title: Crochet pockets
subtitle: Adding attached or integral pockets to a crochet garment
excerpt: Crochet pockets are either worked separately and sewn onto the finished garment, or built in as part of the main fabric by working a pocket opening into the body. The attached method is easier to position; the integral method sits flatter and looks more polished.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: A separate pocket piece sewn onto the surface of a finished garment. The three closed sides are sewn to the garment; the top edge is left open.
A pocket worked into the body of a garment by holding aside the body stitches at the pocket position, working the pocket lining separately, then rejoining to the body stitches and continuing.

content.text: A crochet pocket is either a
patch pocket
sewn on after the garment is complete, or an
in-seam pocket

worked into the body as part of the main fabric. The patch method is more forgiving because you can position it exactly where you want it after the garment is assembled. The in-seam method sits flatter and is more traditional in crochet garments.
What you need

items.name: Matching yarn
items.note: Use the same yarn as the garment for the pocket piece to match the tension and appearance.

items.name: Crochet hook to match the garment
Tapestry needle
items.note: For sewing on a patch pocket or closing the pocket lining seams

items.name: Stitch markers
items.note: For marking the pocket position on the body

items.name: Pins
items.note: For holding the patch pocket in position before sewing

content.text: Method 1: patch pocket
Work the pocket piece to the required dimensions: width and depth in the same stitch and hook as the garment body.
Work one row of double crochet (UK) along the top edge of the pocket piece as a neat facing. Fasten off.
Mark the pocket position on the garment with pins: mark the four corners. Check the position is level and symmetric against any corresponding pocket on the other side.
Sew the bottom edge and two side edges of the pocket to the garment using mattress stitch or ladder stitch, using a length of matching yarn on the tapestry needle. Leave the top edge open.
Reinforce the top corners by working two or three overcast stitches through both the pocket and garment fabric at each top corner. These points take the most stress in use.
Method 2: in-seam pocket
Work the body to the row where the pocket opening starts. Mark the pocket stitches with stitch markers.
On the pocket opening row, work to the first pocket stitch, then fasten off.
Join yarn at the first pocket stitch and work the pocket lining: work back and forth across only the pocket stitches for the full pocket depth. Fasten off.

Return to the main body stitches. Work across the non-pocket stitches, work across the top of the pocket lining (picking up the top row of pocket lining stitches), and continue to the end of the row. The stitch count returns to the full body count.
Seam the sides of the pocket lining to the wrong side of the body at the pocket edges.
Common problems

items.symptom: The patch pocket is not level, sagging at one corner
items.cause: The pocket was not pinned at all four corners before sewing, or the garment fabric stretched under the sewing tension.
items.fix: Unpick and repin, this time pinning at all four corners and at several points along the bottom edge. Sew with the garment flat on a table.

items.symptom: The in-seam pocket opening looks wide and pulls away from the body
items.cause: The pocket opening row was not secured at the edges, or the pocket is too wide relative to the body stitch count.
items.fix: Work a single crochet reinforcement row up each side of the pocket opening from the right side. This draws the edges back to the body.

items.symptom: The patch pocket top edge is curling forward
items.cause: The facing row was worked at too loose a tension.
items.fix: Work the facing row at a tighter tension or with a hook one size smaller than the body. A single row of slip stitch along the very edge also holds it down.

content.text: What to try next
A patch pocket on a cardigan is the easiest first project. Work the pocket, finish the edges, and pin it to the garment before sewing it on. Placement can be adjusted before any stitching is done.
